title: Abena Buys a Piece of a Company

pages.text: During the school holidays in Accra, thirteen-year-old Abena and her cousin Kwaku walked with Auntie Esi past a busy fruit-processing factory and a major bank on Independence Avenue. ‘Auntie Esi,’ asked Abena, ‘who owns giant companies like these? Does one rich person own the whole building?’ Auntie Esi smiled. ‘Actually, Abena, thousands of ordinary Ghanaians—including teachers, nurses and my own family—own small pieces of public companies!’
sentences: During the school holidays in Accra, thirteen-year-old Abena and her cousin Kwaku walked with Auntie Esi past a busy fruit-processing factory and a major bank on Independence Avenue.
‘Auntie Esi,’ asked Abena, ‘who owns giant companies like these?
Does one rich person own the whole building?’ Auntie Esi smiled.
‘Actually, Abena, thousands of ordinary Ghanaians—including teachers, nurses and my own family—own small pieces of public companies!’
pages.alt: Abena and Kwaku walk with Auntie Esi along a clean Accra avenue past modern commercial buildings.

pages.text: At her office, Auntie Esi drew a giant circle divided into equal slices like a pie. ‘When a large company needs capital to build new factories or branches, it can list on the Ghana Stock Exchange—the GSE,’ she explained. ‘The company’s ownership is divided into thousands or millions of equal units called shares, or stocks. When you buy a share through a licensed broker, you become a part-owner, or shareholder, of that real business.’
sentences: At her office, Auntie Esi drew a giant circle divided into equal slices like a pie.
‘When a large company needs capital to build new factories or branches, it can list on the Ghana Stock Exchange—the GSE,’ she explained.
‘The company’s ownership is divided into thousands or millions of equal units called shares, or stocks.
When you buy a share through a licensed broker, you become a part-owner, or shareholder, of that real business.’
pages.alt: Auntie Esi draws a pie chart divided into small slices on a whiteboard while Abena and Kwaku watch attentively.

pages.text: ‘How does a shareholder earn money from a stock?’ asked Kwaku. ‘In two possible ways,’ said Auntie Esi. ‘First, if the company makes a strong profit, its board may share part of that profit with shareholders as a cash payment called a dividend. Second, if the business grows more valuable over time, the price of your share can rise above what you paid—a capital gain. Remember, though: neither dividends nor price increases are guaranteed!’
sentences: ‘How does a shareholder earn money from a stock?’ asked Kwaku.
‘In two possible ways,’ said Auntie Esi.
‘First, if the company makes a strong profit, its board may share part of that profit with shareholders as a cash payment called a dividend.
Second, if the business grows more valuable over time, the price of your share can rise above what you paid—a capital gain.
Remember, though: neither dividends nor price increases are guaranteed!’
pages.alt: Auntie Esi holds up two coloured cards illustrating a dividend coin pouch and a rising share chart alongside a warning sign for risk.

pages.text: ‘Wait—can a share price go down too?’ asked Abena carefully. ‘Yes,’ said Auntie Esi seriously. ‘If a company faces high costs, poor management or tough economic times, its share price can fall below what you paid, causing a capital loss if you sell. That is why investing in stocks carries market risk, and why you should never invest money you will need next week for school fees or food.’
sentences: ‘Wait—can a share price go down too?’ asked Abena carefully.
‘Yes,’ said Auntie Esi seriously.
‘If a company faces high costs, poor management or tough economic times, its share price can fall below what you paid, causing a capital loss if you sell.
That is why investing in stocks carries market risk, and why you should never invest money you will need next week for school fees or food.’
pages.alt: Abena studies a chart where one company’s line dips downward while Auntie Esi explains market risk.

pages.text: ‘Is there another way to invest besides buying shares?’ asked Abena. ‘Yes—bonds!’ said Auntie Esi. ‘When you buy a bond from the government or a company, you are not buying ownership. Instead, you are lending money for a fixed period, and the borrower promises to pay you regular interest and return your original principal at maturity. Bonds are generally steadier than stocks, though they still carry risks such as inflation or borrower difficulties.’
sentences: ‘Is there another way to invest besides buying shares?’ asked Abena.
‘Yes—bonds!’ said Auntie Esi.
‘When you buy a bond from the government or a company, you are not buying ownership.
Instead, you are lending money for a fixed period, and the borrower promises to pay you regular interest and return your original principal at maturity.
Bonds are generally steadier than stocks, though they still carry risks such as inflation or borrower difficulties.’
pages.alt: Auntie Esi contrasts a stock ownership certificate icon with a bond loan-and-interest calendar icon.

pages.text: ‘Why not just leave all our money in a wooden box under the bed for ten years so it never drops?’ asked Kwaku. ‘Because of inflation,’ explained Auntie Esi. ‘Inflation is the general rise in prices over time. If a textbook costs fifty cedis today and inflation makes it cost eighty cedis in a few years, fifty cedis sitting idle in a box loses purchasing power! Thoughtful investing helps savings grow faster than inflation over the long term.’

‘Inflation is the general rise in prices over time.
If a textbook costs fifty cedis today and inflation makes it cost eighty cedis in a few years, fifty cedis sitting idle in a box loses purchasing power!
Thoughtful investing helps savings grow faster than inflation over the long term.’
pages.alt: Kwaku compares a single basket of goods today with a smaller basket in the future to see how inflation reduces purchasing power.

pages.text: To test what they had learned, Auntie Esi gave Abena and Kwaku a fictional one-thousand-cedi classroom portfolio challenge. ‘Never put all your eggs in one basket!’ she reminded them. ‘Spreading money across different investments is called diversification. Let us split our one thousand cedis across three choices: four hundred cedis in Company A stock, two hundred cedis in Company B stock, and four hundred cedis in a one-year bond paying fifteen percent interest.’
sentences: To test what they had learned, Auntie Esi gave Abena and Kwaku a fictional one-thousand-cedi classroom portfolio challenge.
‘Never put all your eggs in one basket!’ she reminded them.
‘Spreading money across different investments is called diversification.

Let us split our one thousand cedis across three choices: four hundred cedis in Company A stock, two hundred cedis in Company B stock, and four hundred cedis in a one-year bond paying fifteen percent interest.’
pages.alt: Abena and Kwaku arrange ten paper hundred-cedi tokens into three separate baskets on the desk to diversify their portfolio.

pages.text: They tracked a full year of real-world economic scenarios. Company A, a well-run food processor, grew its share value from four hundred cedis to four hundred and thirty cedis and paid a twenty-cedi dividend—totalling four hundred and fifty cedis! Meanwhile, Company B faced shipping delays, and its shares dropped from two hundred cedis down to one hundred and eighty cedis—a twenty-cedi loss.
sentences: They tracked a full year of real-world economic scenarios.
Company A, a well-run food processor, grew its share value from four hundred cedis to four hundred and thirty cedis and paid a twenty-cedi dividend—totalling four hundred and fifty cedis!
Meanwhile, Company B faced shipping delays, and its shares dropped from two hundred cedis down to one hundred and eighty cedis—a twenty-cedi loss.
pages.alt: Abena and Kwaku use a calculator to record Company A growing to 450 cedis while Company B drops to 180 cedis.

pages.text: Then they checked Basket 3: the four-hundred-cedi bond at fifteen percent interest earned sixty cedis, growing to four hundred and sixty cedis! Kwaku added all three baskets together: four hundred and fifty cedis plus one hundred and eighty cedis plus four hundred and sixty cedis equalled one thousand and ninety cedis—a net gain of ninety cedis, or nine percent! ‘Even though Company B fell,’ Abena beamed, ‘diversification protected our portfolio!’

Kwaku added all three baskets together: four hundred and fifty cedis plus one hundred and eighty cedis plus four hundred and sixty cedis equalled one thousand and ninety cedis—a net gain of ninety cedis, or nine percent!
‘Even though Company B fell,’ Abena beamed, ‘diversification protected our portfolio!’
pages.alt: Abena and Kwaku high-five as their three diversified baskets total 1,090 cedis on the calculator.

pages.text: Just then, Kwaku showed Auntie Esi a flashy message on a phone promising: ‘Send 200 cedis today and double your money to 400 cedis in 48 hours—guaranteed!’ Auntie Esi’s expression turned firm. ‘Delete that immediately, Kwaku! In Ghana, legitimate investment firms and the Ghana Stock Exchange are regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission—SEC Ghana. Anyone promising huge, instant, risk-free returns is running a Ponzi scam or fraud!’

In Ghana, legitimate investment firms and the Ghana Stock Exchange are regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission—SEC Ghana.
Anyone promising huge, instant, risk-free returns is running a Ponzi scam or fraud!’
pages.alt: Auntie Esi warns Kwaku and Abena to reject a suspicious "double your money in 48 hours" phone message.

pages.text: ‘How does a young person start safely when they are still under eighteen?’ asked Abena. ‘First,’ said Auntie Esi, ‘your family keeps an emergency fund in a safe bank or susu account for sudden needs. Second, because minors under eighteen cannot open a brokerage account alone, a parent or guardian can open a regulated trust or junior investment account with a licensed broker until you reach adulthood.’
sentences: ‘How does a young person start safely when they are still under eighteen?’ asked Abena.
‘First,’ said Auntie Esi, ‘your family keeps an emergency fund in a safe bank or susu account for sudden needs.

Second, because minors under eighteen cannot open a brokerage account alone, a parent or guardian can open a regulated trust or junior investment account with a licensed broker until you reach adulthood.’
pages.alt: Auntie Esi shows Abena and her parents how a regulated junior investment account works alongside a family emergency savings jar.

pages.text: On the bus ride home, Abena looked out at the busy shops, farms and factories of Ghana with brand-new eyes. She did not just see places to buy snacks anymore—she saw enterprises she could study, build, and one day help own through patient, disciplined investing.

activities.question: What is the main difference between buying a stock (share) and buying a bond?
options: A stock makes you a part-owner; a bond is lending money for interest
A stock is only for banks; a bond is only for primary school pupils
A stock never changes price; a bond makes you the company president
activities.explanation: Shares (stocks) represent part-ownership in a company, whereas bonds are loans that pay interest over a set period.

activities.definition: Spreading money across different investments to reduce overall risk
distractors: Putting every cedi you own into a single company stock
Spending all your savings before prices rise

activities.question: In the 1,000-cedi portfolio (Stock A → 450, Stock B → 180, Bond → 460), what was the final total?
options: 1,090 cedis (a net gain of 90 cedis, or 9%)
activities.explanation: 450 + 180 + 460 = 1,090 cedis, which is 90 cedis (9%) more than the starting 1,000 cedis despite Stock B falling.

activities.question: Why did Auntie Esi tell Kwaku to delete the message promising to double 200 cedis in 48 hours?
options: Huge, instant, "guaranteed" returns are a warning sign of a scam
Real investments only work on Sundays
Two hundred cedis is too much money to invest
activities.explanation: Legitimate investments carry risk and grow over time under SEC Ghana regulation; "double your money in 48 hours" is a classic Ponzi/fraud red flag.

activities.prompt: Order the smart steps of responsible investing from the story.
items: Build an emergency savings fund first for short-term and urgent needs.
Learn how stocks, bonds, risk and diversification work.
Invest patiently through SEC-regulated accounts and avoid quick-money scams.

activities.prompt: Why does patient investing require self-control and critical thinking when someone promises "easy fast money"?
